article_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in Teaching and Learning Processes at the K-12 Level: A Systematic Review
citation: Marzano, D. (2025). Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in Teaching and Learning Processes at the K-12 Level: A Systematic Review. Technology, Knowledge and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10758-025-09853-7
title: TPACK model as a bridge between AI theory and practical application in teaching
description: The review presents the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) model, introduced by Mishra and Koehler, as "a fundamental element for bridging the gap between AI theory and its practical application, emphasizing the integration of technological, pedagogical and content knowledge". On this basis the review argues teacher training must be renewed to include these aspects, going beyond simply teaching technical skills and encouraging critical reflection on how technology affects the learning process and teaching practices.
requirements: Teacher training that integrates technological, pedagogical and content knowledge rather than technical skills alone
constraints: The review treats TPACK as a framework from prior literature (Mishra and Koehler 2007, 2008), not as an intervention tested here
target_learners: K-12 teachers integrating GAI into teaching practice
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional development for effective AI and GAI integration
examples: The review cites Koehler and Mishra (2009, 2016) and Voogt et al. (2013) among snowball-sampled TPACK studies
key_sources: Marzano, D. (2025). Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in Teaching and Learning Processes at the K-12 Level: A Systematic Review. Technology, Knowledge and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10758-025-09853-7

article_title: AI-based digital cheating at university, and the case for new ethical pedagogies
citation: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y
title: Combined Theory of Planned Behaviour and Self-Efficacy account of AI-era cheating
description: The article combines Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behaviour with Bandura's Self-Efficacy Theory to explain student decisions to cheat with AI. TPB explains how "attitudes towards cheating, peer influence, and perceived ability to avoid detection" contribute to cheating decisions, while Self-Efficacy Theory explains how beliefs about competence shape perceived control. The combined account holds that a key aspect of cheating is "the interaction between technology's ease of misuse and the individual factors that influence students' choices". The article uses it to argue that banning technologies alone does not deal with the problem at source.
requirements: Understanding both motivational factors (attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioural control) and individual confidence in academic ability and AI-tool use
constraints: Self-Efficacy Theory does not factor in variables in the external environment or deal specifically with cheating, as the article states
The article sets aside external-to-the-student factors such as variable quality of tuition for reasons of space
target_learning_goals: ethical decision-making about AI tool use
examples: The article applies the combined account to argue that a student confident in using AI tools might see less risk of getting caught, increasing the likelihood of dishonesty
key_sources: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y

article_title: Evaluation Indicator System for AI Certificate Programs
citation: Zijing Wu and Qiang Li. (2026). Evaluation indicator system for AI certificate programs. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00604-x
title: TPACK-extended five-dimension evaluation framework for AI certificate programs
description: The article extends the TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) into program-level credential evaluation by mapping five criteria dimensions onto TPACK components: curriculum design as CK, instructional implementation as PK, technical support as TK, faculty competence as the integrative TPACK core, and a newly added Cross-Cultural Adaptability dimension as TPACK-Extended. The framework comprises three hierarchical layers—Goal (A), Criteria (B1–B5), and Indicators (S1–S20)—operationalized through 20 indicators refined via Delphi consultation. It is used to structure AHP-FAHP weighting of pedagogical transformation potential. The article states the framework "extended TPACK by adding the Cross-Cultural Adaptability dimension (B5)".
requirements: Expert panel input (the article used a stratified purposive sample of 18 experts within the 15–20 range recommended by Saaty for AHP studies) and Delphi refinement of indicators
constraints: The study captures expert perceptions of pedagogical transformation potential, not empirical observations of actual teaching practices; AHP weights represent normative priorities rather than descriptive evidence
target_learners: higher education students in AI certificate programs
target_learning_goals: AI competency development, pedagogical transformation of AI credential programs
examples: The framework was instantiated as Table 1, an indicator system with 9-level Saaty scale anchors for 20 sub-indicators coded S1–S20 across criteria layers B1–B5.
key_sources: Zijing Wu and Qiang Li. (2026). Evaluation indicator system for AI certificate programs. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00604-x

article_title: Science educators' AI literacy and AI usage in teaching: Implications for post-qualification programs
citation: Nikolai Maurer, Mathea Brückner, Christoph Thyssen, Sebastian Becker-Genschow, Johannes Huwer. (2026). Science educators' AI literacy and AI usage in teaching: Implications for post-qualification programs. Computers and Education Open 10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100376
title: TPACK adapted for AI (TPACKAI) with two development pathways for in-service science educators
description: The article adapts the TPACK model for AI, using the terms TKAI, TCKAI, TPKAI, and TPACKAI, and proposes two pathways for in-service teachers to develop TPACKAI. Path A enriches existing pedagogical content knowledge with AI-related technological knowledge (TKAI), so that teachers "can thus enable teachers to use AI efficiently as a tool for the preparation and follow-up of lessons". Path B builds knowledge of AI's role in the science subjects (TCKAI) and combines it with PCK so teachers can use AI as subject matter. The article classifies the measured general AI literacy as TKAI and TPKAI.
requirements: In-service teachers already possess AI-independent teaching competencies (PK, PCK, CK) from training and professional experience, which the pathways build on
constraints: The TPACK model's limitations regarding generative AI must be considered; the article notes it needs extension to socio-cultural and ethical aspects as in the DPACK model
Further research is needed to test the two pathways and define the competencies of subject-specific AI literacy
target_learning_goals: using AI as a tool for lesson preparation, follow-up, and individualized support
using AI as subject matter in science lessons
examples: The study assessed teachers' general AI literacy with the Hornberger et al. test and interpreted the scores as indicating the presence of TPKAI and TKAI
Fig. 6 depicts the TPACK model adapted for AI with the two possible pathways to support TPACKAI development among in-service teachers
key_sources: Nikolai Maurer, Mathea Brückner, Christoph Thyssen, Sebastian Becker-Genschow, Johannes Huwer. (2026). Science educators' AI literacy and AI usage in teaching: Implications for post-qualification programs. Computers and Education Open 10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100376

article_title: Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom
citation: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3
title: Teaching Proficiency through Reading and Storytelling (TPRS) method
description: TPRS, developed by Ray and Seely based on Total Physical Response, is a foreign and second language teaching approach emphasising ample clear target language input, high-frequency vocabulary, and collaborative story creation in a stress-free environment. "The method typically involves three key steps: introducing vocabulary through physical movements, collaboratively creating stories through questioning and student engagement, and reading and retelling the stories." In this study TPRS was the curricular vehicle for inclusive pedagogy within MTSS.
requirements: Pairing each vocabulary word with a corresponding physical movement so students can demonstrate comprehension kinaesthetically before being required to speak
constraints: The article notes concerns about scalability of TPRS in large, exam-driven classrooms, and that collaborative storytelling may conflict with traditional teacher-centred approaches prevalent in many Asian classrooms
target_learners: elementary EFL learners, including struggling and neurodiverse students not yet ready to speak
examples: The teacher created a recurring invisible character, Muder, that students named and voted on, which became popular in TPRS stories and student work throughout the year
key_sources: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3

article_title: Teachers’ Attitudes Toward Bullying and Intervention Responses: A Systematic and Meta-analytic Review
citation: Dawes, M., Malamut, S. T., Guess, H., & Lohrbach, E. (2024). Teachers' Attitudes Toward Bullying and Intervention Responses: A Systematic and Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09951-5
title: Theory of Planned Behavior applied to teachers' bullying intervention responses
description: The review is guided by the Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen), in which "behavior is guided by intentions which are influenced by (1) attitudes toward the behavior, (2) subjective norms, and (3) self-efficacy beliefs." Applied to bullying, teachers' intervention intentions are assumed to be guided by their attitudes toward bullying, subjective norms for intervening, and self-efficacy for intervening. The framework's utility is that each component is assumed malleable and thus targetable through intervention efforts. The review tests the attitude–response link this framework predicts.
requirements: Studies must measure teachers' attitudes toward bullying and an outcome measure assessing teachers' intervention response to bullying, and report the association between them.
constraints: The review addresses the attitude component's association with responses; subjective norms and self-efficacy components are covered by other reviews it cites.
target_learning_goals: responding appropriately to bullying and victimization incidents
key_sources: Dawes, M., Malamut, S. T., Guess, H., & Lohrbach, E. (2024). Teachers' Attitudes Toward Bullying and Intervention Responses: A Systematic and Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09951-5

article_title: The decision of African American students to complete high school: An application of the theory of planned behavior.
citation: Davis, L., Ajzen, I., Saunders, J., & Williams, T. (2002). The decision of African American students to complete high school: An application of the theory of planned behavior. Journal of Educational Psychology, 94(4), 810–819. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.94.4.810
title: TPB-based student questionnaire administered early in the second year of high school
description: A questionnaire grounded in the theory of planned behavior was completed by male and female high-school students aged 14 to 17 (N=166) early in their second year. It measured the TPB constructs predicting intentions to complete the year, which the article reports were "accurately predicted from attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control". It functions as an early assessment instrument for completion-relevant beliefs in this longitudinal study.
requirements: Administration early in students' second year, before completion intentions solidify
constraints: Validated here only with African American students aged 14 to 17 in one longitudinal study
target_learners: Male and female African American high-school students aged 14 to 17
target_learning_goals: Predicting intentions to complete the school year
key_sources: Davis, L., Ajzen, I., Saunders, J., & Williams, T. (2002). The decision of African American students to complete high school: An application of the theory of planned behavior. Journal of Educational Psychology, 94(4), 810–819. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.94.4.810

article_title: Designing teacher professional development programs to support a rapid shift to digital
citation: Heap, T., Thompson, R., & Fein, A. (2021). Designing teacher professional development programs to support a rapid shift to digital. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 35–38. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09863-5
title: Philipsen et al.'s framework of key components and categories of an effective TPD for OBL
description: The article presents the reviewed meta-aggregative analysis as offering "a conceptual framework of key components and categories of an effective TPD for OBL" that teacher professional developers can use "as a lens" to create and build upon new initiatives. The categories identified as most impacting a shift to digital are "support and feedback from learning technologists, financial sustainability, program goals and procedures, changes in teachers' skills and attitudes, relevance and evaluation of the TPD program, and support among institutional leadership."
requirements: TPD programs must be designed around the framework's components, including support and feedback from learning technologists and clear program goals and procedures
constraints: The framework synthesizes research papers published between 2004 and 2015, before the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learners: faculty and teachers preparing for online and blended instruction
target_learning_goals: online and blended teaching skills and attitudes
examples: The article's course-in-a-box initiative incorporates categories and guidelines highlighted by Philipsen et al., such as support and feedback from learning technologists, flexibility and sustainability, and clear program goals and procedures
key_sources: Heap, T., Thompson, R., & Fein, A. (2021). Designing teacher professional development programs to support a rapid shift to digital. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 35–38. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09863-5

article_title: The IT2 Survey: contextual knowledge (XK) influences on teacher candidates’ intention to integrate technology
citation: Buss, R. R., Lindsey, L., Foulger, T. S., Wetzel, K., & Pasquel, S. (2017). Assessing a technology infusion approach in a teacher preparation program. International Journal of Technology in Teaching and Learning, 13(1), 33-44. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+a+technology+infusion+approach+in+a+teacher+preparation+program
title: TPACK framework for teacher technology integration knowledge
description: Mishra and Koehler's Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework undergirded the program's technology infusion and research efforts. Building on Shulman's blending of content and pedagogical knowledge, it holds that integration requires "strong content knowledge (CK), pedagogical knowledge (PK), and technology knowledge (TK)" woven together into PCK, TCK, TPK, and TPACK. The program aligned infused courses to ISTE-T standards within this framework.
requirements: Teachers must develop and seamlessly weave together content, pedagogical, and technological knowledge bases
examples: The teacher preparation program infused technology-integration assignments, objectives, and lessons into 16 methods courses across five programs, aligned to the ISTE-T
key_sources: Buss, R. R., Lindsey, L., Foulger, T. S., Wetzel, K., & Pasquel, S. (2017). Assessing a technology infusion approach in a teacher preparation program. International Journal of Technology in Teaching and Learning, 13(1), 33-44. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+a+technology+infusion+approach+in+a+teacher+preparation+program

article_title: Factors shaping faculty online teaching competencies during the Covid-19 pandemic
citation: Trevisan, O., De Rossi, M., Christensen, R., Knezek, G., & Smits, A. (2023). Factors shaping faculty online teaching competencies during the Covid-19 pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10197-1
title: Faculty online-teaching competence as dispositions and environmental conditions framed by the Theory of Planned Behavior and the Integrated Model of Behavior Prediction
description: The article frames faculty competence for online teaching as a multifaceted attribute combining knowledge, skills, pedagogical expertise and "sound pedagogical-technological dispositions including motivation and confidence in one's competence, or self-efficacy". It uses the socio-psychological Theory of Planned Behavior combined with the Integrated Model of Behavior Prediction, which "describes behavior through an antecedent of intentions that vary with attitude, perceived norms, and self-efficacy". Internal factors (dispositions, enthusiasm, resolutions) and external factors (institutional support, training) are treated as antecedents of competent online-teaching behavior, and the study's cluster factors map onto this framework.
requirements: Competent online-teaching behavior is understood as requiring both internal dispositions and external environmental conditions to be addressed together
constraints: The framework is applied to higher education faculty in education departments during the Covid-19 pandemic transition
target_learning_goals: competence for online teaching and technology integration
examples: The study measured Enthusiasm (ease/usefulness of OT), Resolutions to use OT, and perceived institutional Support as observable indicators of the framework's internal and external factors
key_sources: Trevisan, O., De Rossi, M., Christensen, R., Knezek, G., & Smits, A. (2023). Factors shaping faculty online teaching competencies during the Covid-19 pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10197-1

article_title: Teachers’ role in digitalizing education: an umbrella review
citation: Olivia Wohlfart, Ingo Wagner. (2022). Teachers' role in digitalizing education: an umbrella review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-022-10166-0
title: TPACK framework as the dominant theoretical lens in reviews of teachers' digitalization role
description: The Technological-Pedagogical-Content-Knowledge (TPACK) model, introduced by Mishra and Koehler, acknowledges the complexity of teaching by "differentiating seven knowledge domains in the interplay of technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge." In this umbrella review it was the most applied framework: eight of the 23 reviews based their work specifically on TPACK, and 10 of the 14 reviews focused on digital literacy applied it. The reviews examined TPACK's publication development, knowledge-domain delineation, measurement, context, and model development.
requirements: Clear definitions and operationalization of the individual knowledge domains, which the reviewed reviews find rare, for further developing the model and survey instruments
constraints: Four of the TPACK-focused reviews acknowledge that clear definition and delineation of individual knowledge domains is rare and nearly impossible
Context is treated mostly marginally, as a limitation or area for further research
examples: Eight reviews specifically focus on the TPACK framework, examining publication development, distinction of knowledge domains, measurement, context, and model development (Table 2).
key_sources: Olivia Wohlfart, Ingo Wagner. (2022). Teachers' role in digitalizing education: an umbrella review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10166-0

article_title: Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies
citation: Florence Martin, Siyu Long, Katy Haywood, Kui Xie. (2025). Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10550-6
title: Technology-Personal-Environment (TPE) framework for organizing digital distraction research
description: The TPE framework, adapted from the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework for individual-level technology adoption, organizes digital distraction into three dimensions: technological factors (device access, affordances, alerts), personal factors (traits, motives, boredom, physical conditions), and environmental factors (classroom setting, instructor behavior, instructional activities). The review uses it as its coding structure, mapping causes, consequences, and prevention strategies onto the three dimensions, stating that "the TPE framework provides a comprehensive structure for examining the causes, consequences, and potential intervention strategies for addressing digital distraction in educational settings."
requirements: Studies must code distraction factors into technological, personal, and environmental dimensions for the framework to structure analysis
constraints: The framework was adapted from the organization-level TOE framework, and the review notes only 6 of 26 primary studies used any theoretical or conceptual framework
examples: The review coded all 26 studies' causes, consequences, and prevention strategies into TPE-based categories and presents Fig. 2 as a visual summary mapping findings to the framework
key_sources: Florence Martin, Siyu Long, Katy Haywood, Kui Xie. (2025). Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10550-6

article_title: Describing increasing proficiency in teachers’ knowledge of the effective use of digital technology
citation: Saubern R., Urbach D., Koehler M. & Phillips M. (2020). Describing increasing proficiency in teachers’ knowledge of the effective use of digital technology. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103784
title: TPACK Confidence and TPACK Usefulness construct maps describing increasing proficiency
description: The article develops two construct maps — one for TPACK Confidence and one for TPACK Usefulness — that qualitatively describe increasing proficiency in teachers' knowledge of effective technology use. Each map divides the Rasch-derived scale into five bands of equal length (two logits each, starting at -2.0 logits) and describes what teachers in each band typically believe or feel confident about regarding using ICT to support student learning of content. The maps provide 'an inferred typical order of acquisition' of aspects of the construct as respondents move from low to high proficiency.
requirements: Data from a TPACK survey tool analyzed via partial credit Rasch analysis to generate person-item maps
constraints: Based on self-report survey data from a single instrument (TTF TPACK Survey), which the authors note takes a particular approach to measuring TPACK
target_learning_goals: Understanding what it means to have more or less TPACK Confidence and TPACK Usefulness
examples: The TPACK Confidence map describes teachers in Band 5 as extremely confident supporting students to 'actively construct knowledge that integrates curriculum areas' while Band 1 teachers are only moderately confident about some aspects and less confident about others
key_sources: Saubern R., Urbach D., Koehler M. & Phillips M. (2020). Describing increasing proficiency in teachers’ knowledge of the effective use of digital technology. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103784

article_title: Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics Education Research: A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses
citation: Young, J.R. (2016). Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics education research: A systematic review of meta-analyses. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 2(1), 19-29. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.2.1.19
title: TPACK framework as an analytic lens for technology-enhanced mathematics instruction
description: The Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, an extension of Shulman's PCK, holds that technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge afford and constrain one another at their intersections; the article states that "Mishra and Koehler (2008) suggest that the intersection of PCK, TCK, and TPK is TPACK." The review uses TPACK to interpret the most salient moderators of effects across meta-analyses and concludes the framework functions as "an analytic tool to identify and categorize moderator variables in meta-analysis of technology -enhanced mathematics learning." It also notes the framework may not apply one-to-one within mathematics.
requirements: Teacher knowledge must integrate technological, pedagogical, and content considerations rather than treating the technology tool as the primary catalyst
constraints: The article states that within mathematics the TPACK framework "may not be applied in a one -to-one fashion" and that the constructs most salient in a given context should be assessed; TPACK is reported as the least stable construct to measure across in-service and pre-service teachers
examples: The review categorized the 13 meta-analyses' technologies by didactical functionality and mapped the five emergent moderators onto TPK, TCK, and TPACK
key_sources: Young, J.R. (2016). Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics education research: A systematic review of meta-analyses. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 2(1), 19-29. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.2.1.19

article_title: Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education.
citation: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1
title: TPACK model as framework for effective technology-integrated teaching
description: The review draws on Mishra and Koehler's TPACK model, which "describes the intersection of pedagogical, technological, and content knowledge necessary for effective teaching." The model includes seven forms of knowledge intersection: pedagogical knowledge, content knowledge, technological knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, technological pedagogical knowledge, technological content knowledge, and technological pedagogical content knowledge. The review uses this framework to analyze how faculty integrate technology with pedagogy and content in higher education teaching.
requirements: Faculty must develop technological skills and stay updated on technology-related topics
constraints: Framework applied to higher education context in this review
target_learning_goals: effective integration of technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge in teaching
key_sources: Suyo-Vega JA, Fernández-Bedoya VH, Meneses-La-Riva ME. (2024). Beyond traditional teaching: a systematic review of innovative pedagogical practices in higher education. F1000Research. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.143392.1

article_title: The Evaluation of Conceptual Learning and Epistemological Beliefs on Physics Learning by Think-Pair-Share
citation: Gok, T. (2018). The evaluation of conceptual learning and epistemological beliefs on physics learning by think-pair-share. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 4(1), 69-80. https://www.jeseh.net
title: Think-pair-share rests on Bandura's social cognitive theory plus interactive engagement, cooperative learning and wait-time, with five cooperative-learning components
description: The article locates TPS theoretically by stating that "The theoretical framework of think -pair-share instructional strategy depends on Bandura's social co gnitive theory", which explains relationships between behaviors, personal factors, and environmental factors, and that TPS "consists of  several theoretical bases including interactive engagement, cooperative learning, and wait -time". Like peer instruction, TPS is treated as cooperative learning, whose five components are positive interdependence, face-to-face promotive interaction, individual accountability, interpersonal and small group skills, and group processing.
requirements: Cooperative learning functioning requires the five components: positive interdependence, face-to-face promotive interaction, individual accountability, interpersonal and small group skills, and group processing
target_learners: university students in introductory physics courses
examples: The article maps Johnson & Johnson's five cooperative-learning components onto TPS pairs, e.g. pairs encouraging and motivating each other's learning reflects face-to-face promotive interaction
key_sources: Gok, T. (2018). The evaluation of conceptual learning and epistemological beliefs on physics learning by think-pair-share. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 4(1), 69-80. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1170940

article_title: Using Personal and Social Responsibility Model for Gaining Leadership Behavior in Students
citation: Filiz, B. (2019). Using personal and social responsibility model for gaining leadership behavior in students. European Journal of Educational Research, 8(1), 157-168. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.8.1.157
title: Teaching Personal and Social Responsibility (TPSR) model with five responsibility levels
description: TPSR is a physical activity curriculum model for youth development that teaches responsibility through five levels: "respect for the rights and feelings of others, effort/participation, self-direction, helping others/leadership and transferring out of the sports hall". The model is implemented through strategies including relational time, awareness talk, physical activity plan, group meeting and self-reflection time, and in leadership development proceeds through stages from learning to take responsibility to transferring out of the sports hall. The study used TPSR as the basis of a 16-lesson leadership program because it includes a leadership/cooperative behavior level.
requirements: Strategies used to help participants practice the levels: relational time, awareness talk, physical activity plan, group meeting and self-reflection time
constraints: The article notes the TPSR program was not actively used in physical education and sports lessons and sports training in Turkey at the time of the study
target_learners: underprivileged youth in physical activity programs
examples: The study transferred one TPSR level per week over the first four weeks, then assigned students leadership tasks such as peer coaching and cross-age education from week 15
key_sources: Filiz, B. (2019). Using personal and social responsibility model for gaining leadership behavior in students. European Journal of Educational Research, 8(1), 157-168. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.8.1.157

article_title: Using Personal and Social Responsibility Model for Gaining Leadership Behavior in Students
citation: Filiz, B. (2019). Using personal and social responsibility model for gaining leadership behavior in students. European Journal of Educational Research, 8(1), 157-168. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.8.1.157
title: TPSR lesson flow of five recurring sections
description: Each TPSR lesson followed a general course flow of five sections: "Relational time, awareness talk, physical activity plan, group meeting and reflection time". The awareness talk raises the day's responsibility level, the physical activity plan embeds it in cooperative activities, and the group meeting and reflection time provide a question-and-answer environment about students' experiences to raise awareness of leadership behaviors. In this study the flow was used across 16 lessons over eight weeks with two lessons per week.
requirements: Group meetings and reflection times in which students share opinions about the leadership behaviors they experienced
target_learners: high school students in physical education
examples: At the end of each lesson, group meetings were held and students were asked to share opinions about the leadership behaviors they had experienced
key_sources: Filiz, B. (2019). Using personal and social responsibility model for gaining leadership behavior in students. European Journal of Educational Research, 8(1), 157-168. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.8.1.157

article_title: Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK
citation: Arwa Ahmed Abdo Qasem, Gandla Viswanathappa. (2016). Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK. Contemporary Educational Technology, 7(3), 264-276. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbspro.2013.09.248
title: TPACK framework as an integrative model of teacher knowledge for technology integration
description: TPACK is a framework describing the interplay of three primary knowledge forms — Content (CK), Pedagogy (PK), and Technology (TK) — needed for effective technology integration. The article treats it as "a type of integrative and transformative knowledge teachers need to be effectively and adequately prepared to integrate in ICT use in the classroom", and uses its four technology-circle categories (TK, TCK, TPK, TPACK) as the measurement basis for its ICT knowledge scale. The framework addresses overemphasis on technological knowledge in ICT courses taught in isolation from subject matter.
requirements: Teachers must understand the nature of knowledge and inquiry in their subject fields for the framework to guide ICT integration
constraints: The article discusses only the four categories found within the Technology circle (Graham et al, 2009), not all seven TPACK categories
target_learning_goals: integrating ICT into classroom teaching and e-course design
examples: The study used a 35-item ICT knowledge scale based on TPACK's four technology dimensions to assess teachers before and after blended or traditional training
key_sources: Arwa Ahmed Abdo Qasem, Gandla Viswanathappa. (2016). Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK. Contemporary Educational Technology, 7(3), 264-276. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbspro.2013.09.248

article_title: Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK
citation: Arwa Ahmed Abdo Qasem, Gandla Viswanathappa. (2016). Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK. Contemporary Educational Technology, 7(3), 264-276. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbspro.2013.09.248
title: 35-item TPACK-based ICT knowledge scale with five-point awareness ratings (Cronbach's alpha 0.846)
description: A knowledge scale measuring teachers' ICT knowledge based on TPACK (Koehler & Mishra, 2006), using only the four technology-related dimensions. It contains 35 items rated on a five-point Likert scale from 0 (Not aware of the components) to 4 (Highly knowledgeable about the components). Two computer-technology experts validated the Arabic version, a pilot with 22 teachers was conducted, and internal consistency calculated with Cronbach's coefficient alpha was 0.846. The scale served as pretest and posttest for both groups, analyzed with SPSS 17.0.
requirements: Expert validation for the Arabic version
Pilot testing with teachers outside the main sample
constraints: Measures only the four technology-circle TPACK dimensions, not the full seven-category framework
target_learning_goals: assessing awareness and knowledge of ICT components for e-course design
examples: Pretest means showed near-equivalent baseline scores, e.g. experimental TPACK 9.93 versus control 9.03
key_sources: Arwa Ahmed Abdo Qasem, Gandla Viswanathappa. (2016). Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK. Contemporary Educational Technology, 7(3), 264-276. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbspro.2013.09.248

article_title: Impact of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge Based Education Applications on Prospective Teachers' Self-Efficacy Belief Levels toward Science Education
citation: Onder Sensoy, Halil Ibrahim Yildirim. (2018). Impact of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge Based Education Applications on Prospective Teachers' Self-Efficacy Belief Levels Toward Science Education. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 6(10). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i10.3433
title: Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) as the intersection of pedagogy, content and technology
description: TPACK is a teacher competency framework defined as the intersection of pedagogical, content and technological knowledge, going beyond its three components. The article states that "TPACK is a sufficiency of teacher, consisted of the intersection of pedagogy, content and technology" and that it differs from the knowledge of a content expert, a technology expert, or general pedagogical knowledge. The study operationalises TPACK through education applications including mobile applications, simulations, online assessment instruments, animations, virtual laboratories, augmented reality and social media tools used in a teacher-education course.
requirements: Teachers must merge technological and pedagogical knowledge and use it in in-class applications for the framework to translate into teaching practice
constraints: The article notes that integrating technology with education is not as easy as learning technological skills, and that technical computer skills alone do not turn into education skills inside classrooms
target_learners: prospective science teachers in teacher-education programs
examples: In the experimental group, courses were taught with TPACK-based applications and students were asked to use these applications in the materials they were making
key_sources: Onder Sensoy, Halil Ibrahim Yildirim. (2018). Impact of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge Based Education Applications on Prospective Teachers' Self-Efficacy Belief Levels Toward Science Education. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 6(10). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v6i10.3433

article_title: Relationship between Gender and Vocabulary Teaching Methodology among Iranian EFL Children: A Comparison of TPR and Direct Method
citation: Nazgol Nekoui Naeini, Mohsen Shahrokhi. (2016). Relationship between Gender and Vocabulary Teaching Methodology among Iranian EFL Children: A Comparison of TPR and Direct Method. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.1p.60
title: Teach vocabulary to young beginning EFL learners through coordinated speech and physical action (TPR)
description: Total Physical Response is "a language teaching method built around the coordination of speech and action" that teaches language through physical motor activity, making learning "enjoyable and less stressful". The study used it to teach vocabulary to 9-10-year-olds across four units, with students acting out commands, singing songs with actions, and giving instructions to peers.
requirements: Learners must physically act out teacher commands; class seating arranged in a U-shape or circle with the teacher at the centre, as the article describes
constraints: The article states "this method is best used with children or beginners", citing Levine (2005), Hewitt and Linares (1999), and Li (2010)
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary knowledge and word meaning
examples: The TPR group greeted, sang and acted out commands (e.g., "drink the water", "touch your ears", "put your hat off"), with volunteers giving instructions to seated students, as described in the Procedure section
key_sources: Nazgol Nekoui Naeini, Mohsen Shahrokhi. (2016). Relationship between Gender and Vocabulary Teaching Methodology among Iranian EFL Children: A Comparison of TPR and Direct Method. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.1p.60

article_title: Effects of TPRS on Very Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Ketevan Kara, Evrim Eveyik-Aydın. (2019). Effects of TPRS on Very Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.10n.1p.135
title: TPRS three-step storytelling methodology adapted for very young learners
description: TPRS (Teaching Proficiency through Reading and Storytelling) is a language teaching method built on Krashen's Natural Approach and Asher's Total Physical Response that provides "comprehensible input on high frequency vocabulary and structures in a highly contextualized and personalized way". It proceeds through three steps: establishing meaning (pre-teaching via L1 translation, gestures, and PQA), asking a story (storytelling with circling questions and student acting, where "learning is a by-product"), and reading. In this study the steps were adapted for illiterate four-year-olds, replacing the reading step with teacher read-alouds, crafts, songs, and games.
requirements: Target vocabulary selected from the most frequent words of the language
Comprehension checks through circling questions with pre-teaching when comprehension is lacking
constraints: With very young learners the reading step must drop literacy-based activities (reading, translating, rewriting, quizzes) because participants are illiterate
target_learners: very young learners (preschool, pre-compulsory-education children) in EFL settings
target_learning_goals: L2 receptive and productive vocabulary acquisition
examples: Five weekly cycles each used one Raintree red-band storybook, with two hours on establishing meaning, two hours on asking a story with acting and props, and one hour on adapted reading activities
key_sources: Ketevan Kara, Evrim Eveyik-Aydın. (2019). Effects of TPRS on Very Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.10n.1p.135

article_title: Effects of TPRS on Very Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Ketevan Kara, Evrim Eveyik-Aydın. (2019). Effects of TPRS on Very Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.10n.1p.135
title: TPRS is a suitable methodology for teaching vocabulary to very young learners and can be applied in kindergarten EFL curricula
description: Based on the observed gains and the students' enjoyment and motivation during TPRS classes, the article concludes that "TPRS is a sui table methodology for very young learners and can be applied in EFL curricula in kindergartens". It argues TPRS suits this age group because it provides concrete concepts, familiar contexts, and kinesthetic and explorative activities, and suggests a curriculum built on TPRS principles could facilitate teachers' work where no prescribed kindergarten EFL curriculum exists.
requirements: Adaptations for very young learners described in the article (shortened question sets, abundant props, adapted reading stage)
constraints: Evidence base is a single-group, 19-child study without a control group and without statistical significance testing
target_learners: very young learners in kindergarten EFL programs
target_learning_goals: L2 English receptive and productive vocabulary acquisition
examples: The study's five storybook-based weekly cycles with lesson plans following TPRS principles served as a demonstration of how kindergarten English teachers can use the method
key_sources: Ketevan Kara, Evrim Eveyik-Aydın. (2019). Effects of TPRS on Very Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.10n.1p.135

article_title: Research in Mathematics Educational Technology: Current Trends and Futrue Demands
citation: Driskell, S. O., Ronau, R. N., Rakes, C. R., Bush, S. B., Niess, M. L., & Pugalee, D. (2011). Research in mathematics educational technology: Current trends and future demands. In Wiest, L. R., & Lamberg, T. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education (pp. 373-380). Reno, NV: University of Nevada, Reno.
title: TPACK framework with developmental benchmarks
description: The Technology, Pedagogy, and Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework defines the knowledge needed by teachers to integrate technology into the pedagogy of particular subject matter. It consists of descriptive knowledge components (CK, PK, TK) embedded in an educational Context, plus a series of interactions (PCK, TPK, TCK, TPACK). The review notes the framework has been extended to provide developmental benchmarks: recognizing, accepting, adapting, exploring, and advancing.
requirements: Educational Context as a component of the framework
target_learning_goals: Understanding teacher knowledge for technology integration in mathematics
key_sources: Driskell, S. O., Ronau, R. N., Rakes, C. R., Bush, S. B., Niess, M. L., & Pugalee, D. (2011). Research in mathematics educational technology: Current trends and future demands. article_title: Medical Students' Experiences With an Integrated Surgical Suturing Training Module Using Simulation Models and Asynchronous Videos: Interpretive Qualitative Study.
citation: Herrera Alcaíno Álvaro, Vade Martínez Consuelo, Painemal Rivera Benjamín, Serey Torres Daniela, Puentes Bravo Sebastián, Leal Lizama Ignacio, Darrigol Parra Josefina, Riquelme Bahamondes Camila. (2026). Medical Students’ Experiences With an Integrated Surgical Suturing Training Module Using Simulation Models and Asynchronous Videos: Interpretive Qualitative Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/90563
title: The Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework was used as a sensitizing lens to interpret how technological resources, pedagogical strategies, and disciplinary content interacted within participants' experiences.
description: The TPACK framework was used as a sensitizing lens during the later stages of analysis to interpret how technological resources (asynchronous videos), pedagogical strategies (simulation-based instruction), and disciplinary content (suturing techniques) interacted within participants' experiences. The authors state that "this interpretive lens supported the organization and contextualization of themes without constraining the inductive coding process." From a TPACK perspective, the perceived value of the intervention emerged from the interaction among these three components rather than from any single component in isolation.
requirements: Used as a sensitizing lens during the later stages of analysis, not to constrain inductive coding
constraints: Applied as an interpretive lens rather than a coding framework
target_learners: Sixth-year medical students during a surgical internship
key_sources: Herrera Alcaíno Álvaro, Vade Martínez Consuelo, Painemal Rivera Benjamín, Serey Torres Daniela, Puentes Bravo Sebastián, Leal Lizama Ignacio, Darrigol Parra Josefina, Riquelme Bahamondes Camila. article_title: A multistage research on factors influencing and active learning intervention on health literacy of community-residing elderly adults in Nanjing.
citation: Jin Shengxuan, Fa Ruobing, Chao Jianqian, Zhang Na, Bao Min, Wu Yanqian, Wang Leixia, Tan Gangrui. (2025). A multistage research on factors influencing and active learning intervention on health literacy of community-residing elderly adults in Nanjing. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-23394-9
title: TPB-based 12-week active learning health education program for older adults
description: A 12-week community health education program for older adults structured by the Theory of Planned Behaviour, targeting attitudes (weekly health talks), subjective norms (group discussions and collaborative activities) and perceived behavioural control (self-planning sessions and exploratory homework). "Each 90-minute session offered a structured opportunity for older adults to engage in health lectures (30 min), group discussions (30 min), individual daily planning (20 min), and exploratory learning assignments (10 min)", delivered by providers with nursing and public health backgrounds and covering twelve weekly themes from orientation to summarizing.
requirements: A trained primary provider and facilitators with nursing and public health backgrounds, pre-program protocol meetings, and collaboration with community stakeholders on local characteristics, needs and resources
constraints: Evaluated over only three months in a large urban Chinese setting; the control group received pamphlets only, so awareness effects of class participation could not be excluded
target_learning_goals: Health literacy: accessing, assessing and utilizing health information; health knowledge, beliefs, behaviours, skills and intentions
examples: Weekly themes included chronic disease management, nutrition, physical activity, mental health, sleep, medication use, and two health-skills sessions on obtaining reliable health information and using self-monitoring tools
key_sources: Jin Shengxuan, Fa Ruobing, Chao Jianqian, Zhang Na, Bao Min, Wu Yanqian, Wang Leixia, Tan Gangrui. (2025). A multistage research on factors influencing and active learning intervention on health literacy of community-residing elderly adults in Nanjing. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-23394-9

article_title: Exploring the mediating effect of personality traits in the relationship between entrepreneurial intentions and academic performance among students.
citation: Panda Smita, Arumugam Vasumathi. (2023). Exploring the mediating effect of personality traits in the relationship between entrepreneurial intentions and academic performance among students. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0293305
title: Theory of Planned Behavior extended with personality traits as mediators of the entrepreneurial-intention to academic-performance relationship
description: The study uses the Theory of Planned Behavior as its theoretical framework, in which "individuals' intentions to engage in a particular behavior, such as entrepreneurship, are influenced by three key factors: attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control". The article extends this framework by introducing personality traits as potential mediators between entrepreneurial intentions and academic success, seen as factors that can influence the strength or direction of that relationship. The conceptual model (Fig 1) operationalises entrepreneurial intention via attitude, perceived behavioral control, subjective norms, perceived educational support and propensity to act, and academic performance via self-efficacy, self-set goals, academic competence, ability and time management.
requirements: Measurement of entrepreneurial intention, personality traits, and academic performance as distinct latent constructs with adequate reliability and validity
constraints: The descriptive, cross-sectional design does not establish causality
examples: The 175-student survey model measured entrepreneurial intention, personality traits, and academic performance with questionnaire items and tested the mediated pathway via PLS-SEM
key_sources: Panda Smita, Arumugam Vasumathi. (2023). Exploring the mediating effect of personality traits in the relationship between entrepreneurial intentions and academic performance among students. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0293305

article_title: From pedagogical content knowledge toward technological pedagogical content knowledge frameworks and their effectiveness in teaching mathematics: A mapping review.
citation: Habiyaremye HT, Ntivuguruzwa C, Ntawiha P. (2022). From pedagogical toward technological pedagogical content knowledge frameworks and their effectiveness in teaching mathematics: A mapping review. F1000Research 11:1029. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.125073.1
title: TPACK framework: three knowledge domains whose intersections produce technological pedagogical content knowledge
description: TPACK characterizes the knowledge required to teach content with technology, extending Shulman's PCK. In the framework, "Three components (content, pedagogical, and technological) of knowledge intersect": CK and PK yield PCK, CK and TK yield technological content knowledge, and PK and TK yield technological pedagogical knowledge. The review presents this as the most recent major evolution of Shulman's original model, developed in reaction to the lack of theory guiding technology integration into teaching.
requirements: Requires distinguishing content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge, and technological knowledge as separable teacher knowledge domains
constraints: The review presents the framework descriptively from the originating articles; it does not itself test TPACK's predictive validity
target_learners: teachers of mathematics at primary, secondary, and university levels
target_learning_goals: integrating technology into mathematics teaching through combined content, pedagogical, and technological knowledge
examples: The review's Table 2 lists seven TPACK upgrades among the 24 frameworks, including Niess's four aspects of teachers' TPCK and Chai et al.'s revised scaffolded TPACK lesson design model
key_sources: Habiyaremye HT, Ntivuguruzwa C, Ntawiha P. (2022). From pedagogical toward technological pedagogical content knowledge frameworks and their effectiveness in teaching mathematics: A mapping review. F1000Research 11:1029. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.125073.1

article_title: The design and validation of a low-cost trans perineal (TP) prostate biopsy simulator for training: improving trainees' confidence and cognitive targeting skills.
citation: Ong Kelly, Bald Philip, Dryhurst David, Ahmed Saif, Yusuf Gibran Tim, Lunawat Rahul, Sriprasad Seshadri, Thapa Gauri, Tirnoveanu Alice, Webb Richard, Rahman Eqram. (2023). The design and validation of a low-cost trans perineal (TP) prostate biopsy simulator for training: improving trainees’ confidence and cognitive targeting skills. World Journal of Urology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00345-023-04387-y
title: Low-cost colour-coded TP prostate biopsy simulator with immediate physical feedback via coloured cores
description: A bench-top transperineal prostate biopsy simulator built from 3D-printed PLA moulds and tissue-mimicking materials (16% alginate phantom in 0.75% agarose, with a 10 mm × 10 mm lesion of 2% agar and 1% aluminium oxide). Its novel concept is that 'areas for systematic biopsies (anterior, mid and posterior zones) are denoted by different colours', so biopsy cores can be examined retrospectively to identify the segment sampled. The total material cost of each simulator was approximately £7.50.
requirements: Requires a rectal ultrasound probe space and fake perineal skin on the simulator box; lesions must be ultrasound-visible (hyper-echoic) for target biopsy tasks
constraints: Lesions could not be placed in pre-planned areas; their final position was identified once the phantom had been cross-linked
Lesions were made hyper-echoic, which is different from actual lesions which are hypoechoic
target_learners: Urology trainees, from biopsy-naïve novices to registrars and consultants
target_learning_goals: Target lesion identification and sampling on ultrasound
Cognitive targeting skills for transperineal prostate biopsy
examples: The phantom was suspended in a simulator box including a space to replicate the rectum for the rectal ultrasound probe
key_sources: Ong Kelly, Bald Philip, Dryhurst David, Ahmed Saif, Yusuf Gibran Tim, Lunawat Rahul, Sriprasad Seshadri, Thapa Gauri, Tirnoveanu Alice, Webb Richard, Rahman Eqram. (2023). The design and validation of a low-cost trans perineal (TP) prostate biopsy simulator for training: improving trainees’ confidence and cognitive targeting skills. World Journal of Urology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00345-023-04387-y

article_title: Virtual care is growing, but who will train upcoming learners to practice it?
citation: Lee J, Kron F. (2022). Virtual care is growing, but who will train upcoming learners to practice it? Med Educ. 2022;56(12):1155-1157. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14934
title: Theory of Planned Behaviour as an explanatory framework for faculty reluctance to adopt virtual care learner training
description: The commentary applies the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) to explain faculty reluctance to integrate learners into virtual care. TPB "posits that behavioural intention is influenced by three factors": attitude toward a behaviour, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control. For faculty, these three factors with respect to VC learner integration "tends to be negative, making them less inclined to adopt it", so behavioural intention to adopt VC learner training is low.
requirements: The framework requires analysing faculty attitudes, perceived social norms, and perceived behavioural control regarding VC learner training to predict adoption intention.
constraints: The commentary notes that, to its knowledge, no effort has been made to optimise the determinants of VC training to give it positive value for faculty.
target_learners: Clinical faculty supervising learners in virtual care
target_learning_goals: Faculty willingness to integrate learners into virtual care delivery
examples: The commentary maps faculty views of VC as an inferior learning platform to attitude, diminished educational mandate to norms, and disrupted routines and time management challenges to control.
key_sources: Lee J, Kron F. (2022). Virtual care is growing, but who will train upcoming learners to practice it? Med Educ. 2022;56(12):1155-1157. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14934

article_title: Exploring the Impact of a TPSR Program on Transference of Responsibility Goals within a Preschool Setting: An Action Research Study.
citation: Santos Fernando, Miguel Jacinta, Wright Paul M., Sá Cesar, Saraiva Linda. (2020). Exploring the Impact of a TPSR Program on Transference of Responsibility Goals within a Preschool Setting: An Action Research Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17249449
title: Hellison's TPSR model with five responsibility levels as a framework for teaching personal and social responsibility in preschool PE
description: The teaching personal and social responsibility (TPSR) model is an instructional model and teaching philosophy that intentionally teaches personal and social responsibility in and through physical education. It frames developmental goals through responsibility levels: "respect for the rights and feelings of others (level I), effort (level II), self-direction (level III), leadership (IV), and transference of responsibility model goals (level V)". A key pedagogical principle is creating an autonomy-based climate in which children make decisions and take ownership, with the final objective of fostering life skills transfer to other life domains. The study adapted the model's levels, language, and strategies to preschool children's developmental needs.
requirements: Responsibility levels should be defined according to children's developmental needs
Model fidelity procedures such as an implementation checklist and expert consultation
constraints: Typical TPSR programs were conducted with adolescent youth, so responsibility-based strategies should be carefully considered to avoid extrapolations to other educational settings such as preschool
target_learners: preschool children aged four to five
examples: The ESTAR program used a responsibility pyramid for self-assessment, a weekly scoreboard, a ceremony for feedback, and a responsibility card sent home to parents
key_sources: Santos Fernando, Miguel Jacinta, Wright Paul M., Sá Cesar, Saraiva Linda. (2020). Exploring the Impact of a TPSR Program on Transference of Responsibility Goals within a Preschool Setting: An Action Research Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17249449

article_title: Supervisors' intention to observe clinical task performance: an exploratory study using the theory of planned behaviour during postgraduate medical training.
citation: de Jonge Laury P. J. W. M., Mesters Ilse, Govaerts Marjan J. B., Timmerman Angelique A., Muris Jean W. M., Kramer Anneke W. M., van der Vleuten Cees P. M. (2020). Supervisors' intention to observe clinical task performance: an exploratory study using the theory of planned behaviour during postgraduate medical training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02047-y
title: 56-item web-based TPB questionnaire measuring supervisors' intention to perform direct observations
description: A theory-informed instrument developed to measure supervisors' intention to perform direct observations, following the TACT principle to define the behaviour and the Francis et al. (2004) manual for item generation. The article states: "Our 56-item web-based questionnaire (Additional file 1) consisted of three parts, namely a general introduction that contained the definition of the behaviour of interest, five items on demographic variables and 51 TPB statements." Items used 7-point Likert scales except control beliefs, rated on a 100-point scale; internal consistencies of direct measures ranged from 0.65 to 0.92.
requirements: At least 40 items are considered a minimum for TPB research, which drove the questionnaire's length.
Belief-based items must cover 75% of the cumulative frequency of beliefs reported in elicitation focus groups.
constraints: The authors note the survey length may have influenced respondents' acceptance, since response rate tends to be negatively correlated with the number of items.
target_learners: GP supervisors in postgraduate specialty training
target_learning_goals: Measuring attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioural control, past behaviour and intention regarding direct observations of trainees
examples: Pilot tested by 10 GP supervisors after team pre-testing of a preliminary 65-item version; administered between June and October 2017 with a net response rate of 41% (N = 82).
key_sources: de Jonge Laury P. J. W. M., Mesters Ilse, Govaerts Marjan J. B., Timmerman Angelique A., Muris Jean W. M., Kramer Anneke W. M., van der Vleuten Cees P. M. (2020). Supervisors' intention to observe clinical task performance: an exploratory study using the theory of planned behaviour during postgraduate medical training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02047-y
